name: Michael Powell
teaser: Powell's Peeping Tom was so reviled on release that it ended his career — decades later it was re-examined as a masterpiece of British horror.

exploreAction.targetName: The Red Shoes (1948), the ballet sequence
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the 15-minute ballet — Powell cuts between reality and the stage world so seamlessly that you stop being able to tell them apart. That confusion is the point: art consumes the dancer.

name: Vittorio De Sica
teaser: De Sica cast a real unemployed man and his real son for Bicycle Thieves — they'd never acted before, and the film's authenticity rewrote world cinema.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the ending on the street — the father's breakdown in front of his son. De Sica refused to film it in a studio: the crowd is real, and their stares become the film's final verdict.

name: Robert Bresson
teaser: Bresson famously forbade his actors from acting — he called them 'models' and shot take after take until every trace of performance was gone.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch how Bresson films hands instead of faces — the pickpocketing is shown as pure gesture. Notice how the emotion lives in what's NOT acted: stillness, silence, hands.

name: Yasujirō Ozu
teaser: Ozu placed his camera at tatami-mat height — about three feet off the ground — for his entire career, and never once moved it during a scene. His films are the cinema of sitting down.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the elderly couple packing for Tokyo. Ozu cuts straight from face to face with no camera movement and no reaction shots. Notice how the stillness makes every word land harder.

name: Luis Buñuel
teaser: Buñuel's first film, Un Chien Andalou, opens with an eye being slit — he made it to shock the bourgeoisie, and he never really stopped.

exploreAction.targetName: The Discreet Charm of the Bourgeoisie (1972), the first dinner scene
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the first dinner party that never quite happens. Buñuel's joke is that the guests can't eat, and neither can we — the film keeps interrupting itself exactly when satisfaction should arrive.

name: Victor Fleming
teaser: Fleming was the third director on Gone with the Wind — the first two were fired, and he took over mid-production, shooting the film's most famous scenes under impossible pressure.

exploreAction.targetName: Gone with the Wind (1939), the Atlanta fire sequence
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the burning of Atlanta — the fire was real, shot with a dozen cameras and hundreds of extras. Fleming staged the studio's biggest set ever and burned it to the ground in one take.

name: Frank Capra
teaser: Capra's It's a Wonderful Life flopped on release and only became a Christmas classic after the studio's copyright lapsed and TV stations played it for free.

exploreAction.targetName: It's a Wonderful Life (1946), the final 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the ending — George Bailey running through Bedford Falls, discovering he's 'the richest man in town.' Capra's most radical idea: the film's hero is a man who never left his hometown.

name: Howard Hawks
teaser: Hawks worked in every genre — westerns, comedies, noir, war — and said a good movie is 'three great scenes and no bad ones.' He made about 40 of them.

exploreAction.targetName: His Girl Friday (1940), the first 15 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the overlapping dialogue — Hawks had actors talk over each other, a novelty in 1940. The movie moves at the speed of a newsroom; notice how much plot arrives in the first ten minutes.

name: Michael Curtiz
teaser: Curtiz directed Casablanca while the studio was churning out war films — he treated it as just another assignment, and it became one of the most quoted movies ever made.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the refugees, the passport chase, the arrival of Rick. Curtiz establishes an entire world of desperation before his hero says a word. Notice how every character is introduced by their relationship to escape.

name: Elia Kazan
teaser: Kazan directed Streetcar and On the Waterfront, both with Marlon Brando, and trained most of the Method actors who defined 1950s Hollywood.

exploreAction.targetName: On the Waterfront (1954), the taxi scene
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the famous taxi confession — 'I coulda been a contender.' Kazan's camera stays on Brando's face; the scene is a masterclass in Method acting and the reason the film survives its own politics.

name: Nicholas Ray
teaser: Ray's Rebel Without a Cause gave teenage alienation its visual language — James Dean's red jacket and the knife fight are pure Ray.

exploreAction.targetName: Rebel Without a Cause (1955), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Jim Stark drunk in the street, the toy monkey, the family. Ray shot in WarnerColor and widescreen, making teenage angst look operatic. Notice the red jacket: Ray's color code.

name: Alain Resnais
teaser: Resnais's Hiroshima mon amour opened with documentary footage of the bombing, then dissolved into a love story — memory and history tangled in the same frame.

exploreAction.targetName: Hiroshima mon amour (1959), the first 15 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening lovers' exchange over documentary footage. Resnais refuses to show the bomb — only its aftermath, repeated like a memory loop. Notice how the voiceover argues with the images.

name: Michelangelo Antonioni
teaser: Antonioni's L'Avventura booed at Cannes in 1960 — the audience hated that a woman disappears and the film never explains it. It's now a landmark of modernist cinema.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the island sequence where Anna vanishes. Antonioni's radical move: the mystery is never solved, and the film doesn't care. Notice how the landscape shots outlast the characters.

name: Pier Paolo Pasolini
teaser: Pasolini was a poet, novelist, and Marxist before he was a director — his Gospel According to St. Matthew cast a real bricklayer as Jesus.

exploreAction.targetName: The Gospel According to St. Matthew (1964), the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Pasolini shot the gospel in real Italian villages with real faces. The camera is often hand-held and the faces are untrained; it reads like a documentary of a miracle.

name: Bernardo Bertolucci
teaser: Bertolucci was Pasolini's assistant on Accattone — he was 20 when he directed his first feature, and 31 when Last Tango in Paris scandalized the world.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Vittorio's flashback in fascist Rome. Bertolucci's camera glides through rooms and memory with a style that inspired a generation of cinematographers. Notice the shadows and the Mussolini-era architecture.

name: Kenji Mizoguchi
teaser: Mizoguchi's films are almost all about women suffering under male power — his sister was sold into geisha service when he was a child, and he never stopped filming that wound.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the final shot — a long take of the widow at her husband's grave. Mizoguchi held his camera motionless for minutes at a time; the stillness becomes grief you can stand in.

name: Mira Nair
teaser: Nair made Salaam Bombay! with street kids she found in Bombay's red-light district — several of her young actors were real children living on those streets.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Krishna's arrival in the city. Nair shot with non-actors and a documentary crew's patience. Notice how the camera treats the street kids as people, not scenery.

name: Hou Hsiao-hsien
teaser: Hou's films are famous for long takes where almost nothing happens — a train passing, a family at dinner — and audiences either walk out or never leave.

exploreAction.targetName: A City of Sadness (1989), the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening dinner scenes — Hou stages whole conversations in long shots with the camera far away. Notice how you learn the family's history through posture and silence, not close-ups.

name: Edward Yang
teaser: Yang's Yi Yi is a three-hour film about a Taiwanese family that somehow feels like your own — it won him the Best Director prize at Cannes in 2000.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the wedding that opens the film and notice how Yang introduces his whole family through it. The film's famous line — 'we can't know the other half' — is planted in the first half hour.

name: Abbas Kiarostami
teaser: Kiarostami made Taste of Cherry about a man driving around Tehran looking for someone to bury him — the film ends with behind-the-scenes footage of the crew, blurring documentary and fiction.

exploreAction.targetName: Taste of Cherry (1997), the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — a man driving, asking strangers for a favor he won't name. Kiarostami keeps the camera inside the car the whole time. Notice how the landscape becomes a character through the windshield.

name: Emir Kusturica
teaser: Kusturica's Underground won the Palme d'Or by telling Yugoslavia's collapse as a wild, drunken circus — his films move at the speed of a brass band falling downstairs.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the brass band, the tank, the wedding. Kusturica stages chaos as choreography. Notice how every scene is built on music and movement, not dialogue.

name: Krzysztof Kieślowski
teaser: Kieślowski made a film about love, Blue, that barely shows the lovers — he claimed he was done with cinema after the Three Colors trilogy, and he was telling the truth.

exploreAction.targetName: Three Colors: Blue (1993), the first 20 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the car crash that Julie survives. Kieślowski drains the world of color then floods it back, blue by blue. Notice how the camera keeps finding her without her moving.

name: Pedro Almodóvar
teaser: Almodóvar grew up in a poor La Mancha village and moved to Madrid with no money — his films celebrate the outsiders, the loud, the melodramatic, in colors that refuse to be subtle.

exploreAction.targetName: All About My Mother (1999), the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the mother's loss, then her flight to Barcelona. Almodóvar builds a family of strangers. Notice how red appears everywhere: his color code for love and grief.

name: Guillermo del Toro
teaser: Del Toro keeps a 'bleak house' of his own monster memorabilia and admits he makes 'melodramas in monster costumes' — Pan's Labyrinth is a war film wearing a fairy tale.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Ofelia bleeding into the labyrinth, then the fantasy world. Del Toro cuts between the fairy tale and Franco's Spain; notice how the monster and the soldier speak the same language.

name: Alfonso Cuarón
teaser: Cuarón shot Children of Men with a series of long, unbroken takes that required a camera rig built into a car — the film's 4-minute car ambush scene took weeks to rehearse.

exploreAction.targetName: Children of Men (2006), the car ambush scene
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the continuous car ambush take. Cuarón's camera never cuts, so the violence unfolds in real time. Notice how the chaos is choreographed — every bullet has a plan.

name: Alejandro González Iñárritu
teaser: Iñárritu's Birdman looks like one continuous shot — it was actually stitched from dozens of takes with hidden cuts, and the illusion made him the first Mexican director to win Best Picture.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening and try to spot where the hidden cuts are. Iñárritu's fake single-take makes the theater's cramped hallways feel like a fever dream. Notice how the drum score never stops.

name: Park Chan-wook
teaser: Park's Oldboy won the Grand Prix at Cannes and made Korean vengeance cinema famous — its corridor fight is one long side-scrolling shot that took three days to shoot.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the hammer fight in the corridor — one horizontal tracking shot, no cuts. Park blocked it like a video game level. Notice how the hero's exhaustion is part of the choreography.

name: Takashi Miike
teaser: Miike has directed over a hundred films across every genre — including a children's film and the most notorious horror films ever made — often shooting several a year.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the first half — a gentle romance, then the bag, then the phone call. Miike's most famous trick is the tonal turn: notice the exact moment the film stops being kind.

name: Jia Zhangke
teaser: Jia films the places China's economic boom left behind — his movies are a documentary record of a country demolishing itself into the future.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — a state dance troupe in the 1980s practicing in a shabby hall. Jia tracks how clothes, music, and dance change as China changes. Notice the haircuts: that's the timeline.

name: Apichatpong Weerasethakul
teaser: Apichatpong's films mix documentary, memory, and ghosts — Uncle Boonmee, which won the Palme d'Or, features a talking catfish and a dead wife who returns as a glowing ape.

exploreAction.targetName: Uncle Boonmee Who Can Recall His Past Lives (2010), the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening dinner — the dead wife arrives calmly, and no one screams. Apichatpong treats ghosts as neighbors. Notice how the forest sounds do the storytelling.

name: Ryusuke Hamaguchi
teaser: Hamaguchi's Drive My Car won an Oscar for Best International Feature and runs three hours — most of it two people talking in a car. Audiences found it riveting.

exploreAction.targetName: Drive My Car (2021), the first 30 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — the prologue before the title card. Hamaguchi builds grief through small gestures and theater rehearsal. Notice how the car becomes a confessional.

name: Chloé Zhao
teaser: Zhao cast real nomads — not actors — in Nomadland, and lived among them while filming in a van she bought herself.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Fern packing her storage unit into a van. Zhao mixes scripted scenes with real nomads telling their own stories. Notice how the landscape shots give Fern room to breathe.

name: Agnès Varda
teaser: Varda called herself the 'grandmother of the New Wave' — she was filming La Pointe Courte a year before Godard and Truffaut, and she never stopped experimenting until she was 90.

exploreAction.targetName: Cléo from 5 to 7 (1962), the first 25 minutes
exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Cléo waiting for medical results, followed in real time. Varda films her in mirrors and shop windows; notice how the city becomes a clock counting down.

name: Chantal Akerman
teaser: Akerman's Jeanne Dielman is a 3.5-hour film about a woman peeling potatoes and making beds — in 2022, Sight & Sound ranked it the greatest film ever made.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the first half hour — household chores in real time, shot head-on. Akerman's radical claim: domestic labor is worthy of cinema's full attention. Notice when the routine breaks.

name: Jane Campion
teaser: Campion was the first woman to win the Palme d'Or — for The Piano — and the second to be nominated twice for Best Director, for The Power of the Dog.

exploreAction.instruction: Watch the opening — Ada's fingers, the piano on the beach, the storm. Campion tells you her heroine's whole world in the first scene: she is married to her instrument. Notice the mud.
